rv.q: Urie, an inventive comic actor who has headlined as a histrionic Hamlet at the Shakespeare Theater Company in Washington, delivers a commanding performance, flirting and joking his way through scenes as a decadent (coked-up?) playboy with an entourage of flatterers.
This production succeeds by finding and enlivening that pitched battle.
Urie brilliantly embodies Shakespeare's King Richard, infusing him with just enough whimsy and vulnerability to make this manchild pitiable.
Urie also finds ways to signal a sense of irony and cynicism into the portrayal, which, perhaps, is the most successfully modern interpolation into Shakespeare's seldom-produced history play.
The production is an absorbing, compelling and compact one thanks largely to swift pacing from Baldwin and Urie’s multilayered performance.
If you’re on the lookout for something as simple as a Shakespeare production that feels fresh and stirring, this play’s the thing.

Indeed, with such top-tier thespians on hand, one wonders if a “straight” production might have ultimately been more pleasing than watching Baldwin throw a lot of proverbial spaghetti at the wall to enliven the 2 ½-hour show.
And as rendered by the marvelous Michael Urie in the Red Bull Theater’s current messy off-Broadway revival at the Astor Place, he’s every bit the fascinating, flawed figure that Shakespeare intended.
With little of interest characterlogically or politically, the production is hit or miss...
Richard II is thought provoking on a multitude of levels and an astounding production in this iteration.
What ultimately distinguishes this Richard II is its emotional intelligence and stance.
Michael Urie delivers a vulnerable, fascinating, fully committed Richard: pansexual and flippant one moment, thoughtful and self-reflective the next.
Baldwin’s production—which does help clarify what can be muddled political factions—also features a generally high order of verse speaking.
But this Richard II emerges more as an exercise in style than substance, unable to justify why its 1980s glosses enhance our understanding of this story or these characters.

cn.t: Michael Urie captivates in this stylish but divisive 1980s-set revival, with critics praising his commanding performance while splitting on the production's bold modern concept—some finding it accessible and electric, others calling it overly gimmicky.
